rubric.name: Hackathon judging (strict)
rubric.description: Would this write-up hold up in front of the judges, given what is true about the project?
rubric.context:
You judge one hackathon entry from its write-up. facts.json lists everything true about the project; the write-up may
claim nothing beyond it. Be strict: when in doubt, judge it as failing. Each check looks only at the kind of problem
it names; ignore other kinds of problems when judging it.

levels.label: minor
levels.description: A small convenience; the write-up doesn't say who has the problem or why it matters

levels.label: useful
levels.description: A real problem for a named group, but the stakes or the evidence are thin

levels.label: major
levels.description: A serious problem for a clearly named group, with what was actually shown about it

levels.label: unclear
levels.description: Buzzwords instead of a build; you can't tell what was made or whether it works

levels.label: partial
levels.description: A working core is described, but how it works or what was tested is vague

levels.label: solid
levels.description: Says what was built, with what, and what was tested end to end

levels.label: familiar
levels.description: Works like products people already use, and the write-up doesn't say what is different

levels.label: fresh_angle
levels.description: A familiar idea; the write-up hints at what is different but doesn't compare it with what exists

levels.label: new
levels.description: Says what existing options miss, and does something they don't for this group

anchors.overclaims: The write-up claims users, deployments, accuracy, predictions or results that facts.json doesn't contain (for example a percentage, a number of places or people, or AI the project doesn't have)
anchors.honest: Every claim about users, deployments, accuracy and results is in facts.json. Missing sections are judged elsewhere

criteria.name: Opens with what it does and for whom

anchors.missing: The opening is a slogan or a vision, or doesn't name who the project is for
anchors.present: The first paragraph says plainly what the project does and names who it is for

criteria.name: Says what was built at the event and what existed before

anchors.missing: The write-up doesn't separate what the team built during the hackathon from what already existed (code, libraries, hardware)
anchors.present: The write-up lists what was built during the hackathon and names what existed before

criteria.name: Credits the AI tools it used

anchors.missing: facts.json lists an AI tool the team used to build the project, and the write-up doesn't name it and what it was used for
anchors.credited: Every AI tool listed in facts.json is named in the write-up with what it was used for

anchors.missing: No link to a demo video or a live demo
anchors.linked: Links the demo video or live demo from facts.json

anchors.missing: No link to the source code
anchors.linked: Links the public repository from facts.json

anchors.missing: The write-up doesn't say what is unfinished or doesn't work yet
anchors.stated: The write-up names what is unfinished or doesn't work yet, as listed in facts.json

aggregation.formula: honest_n < 0.5 ? 0 : (impact_n * 3 + technical_n * 2 + originality_n) / 6 * (1 + what_for_whom_n + built_during_n + ai_credited_n + demo_n + code_n + limits_n) / 7

gates.message: Claims users, results or accuracy the project doesn't have

evidence.label: entry
evidence.text:
# Tidewatch

Tidewatch texts residents of streets next to small creeks and storm drains when their street is about to flood. A water-level sensor on the storm drain sends an SMS to nearby residents when the water rises past a threshold.

Using an IoT sensor and SMS, Tidewatch delivers alerts within seconds of a reading.

## Built at the hackathon vs. before

Built by our team of 3 during the 36-hour hackathon:
- SMS alert service (FastAPI + Twilio)
- threshold rule that needs 2 readings in a row
- map dashboard of sensor readings
- 3D-printed sensor enclosure

Existed before the event:
- ultrasonic sensor firmware from our earlier open-source university project
- ESP32 board and sensor, bought before the event

## AI tools used

- Claude Code: wrote most of the map dashboard's frontend code.

## Demo

Demo video (2:40): https://video.example.org/tidewatch-demo

We are passionate about making streets safer, and we want to keep building Tidewatch.
